name: Magic Shave

angle.text: Magic Shave is a depilatory powder used to remove body and facial hair quickly, with smooth skin visible right after. It sits alongside Nair and Veet as a non-razor option, and results last until regrowth in a few days.

summary: A chemical depilatory powder that dissolves hair at the skin surface; medical literature records eye injuries and a barium sulfide poisoning case.
note: Published case reports describe a poisoning after ingestion and corneal burns from eye exposure.
currentQuick:
Magic Shave is a brand of chemical depilatory powder. Depilatories remove hair at the skin surface rather than destroying the follicle, so hair grows back.
It appears in the medical literature mainly through case reports of harm: a 1989 mass eye-injury incident aboard a ship and a 2000 case of poisoning after a product containing barium sulfide was swallowed.
How it works: Chemical depilatories break the disulfide bonds in hair keratin so hair can be wiped away; they do not destroy the dermal papilla, so regrowth occurs. Wikipedia lists Magic Shave among powder-form depilatories.
Risks and caveats: A 1989 report described corneal alkali burns in 40 sailors from a powder suspected to be Magic Shave (calcium hydroxide). A 2000 case report described respiratory arrest and dangerous potassium disturbances after a man swallowed a barium sulfide depilatory of this brand.
deepLead:
Magic Shave is a brand of chemical depilatory powder. Wikipedia lists it, alongside Nair and Veet, among depilatory products sold as gels, creams, lotions, aerosols, roll-ons and powders. 
Depilatories break down the keratin in hair so it can be wiped off; because they leave the dermal papilla intact, hair grows back.  The brand appears in the medical literature primarily in case reports of harm.

name: Laser hair-growth helmet/cap

angle.text: Users wear laser caps and helmets for sessions at home in hopes of slowing hair loss and thickening hair in androgenetic alopecia. Low-level laser therapy has been studied for this, with reviews reporting mixed-to-tentative benefit and asking for larger trials.

summary: Wearable low-level laser caps and helmets marketed for androgenetic alopecia; reviews report mixed-to-tentative benefit and call for larger trials.
note: Several devices are FDA-cleared; long-term effects are unknown.
currentQuick:
Laser hair-growth helmets and caps are wearable devices using low-level laser therapy (LLLT) to treat androgenetic alopecia. Some are FDA-cleared, and prices vary widely; one forum user cited about $2,000 for a premium helmet.
Reviews summarised on Wikipedia range from little evidence (2012) to tentative benefit (2015, 2017), with authors calling for larger long-term double-blind trials.
How it works: Low-power red laser light is proposed to act on mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase in follicle cells. The mechanism remains under investigation.
Risks and caveats: Reported side effects are mild pain or skin irritation; long-term effects on skin and hair are unknown. Some devices call for eye protection.
deepLead:
Laser hair-growth helmets and caps are wearable devices that apply low-level laser therapy (LLLT, also called photobiomodulation) to the scalp with the aim of treating androgenetic alopecia. Wikipedia lists hats, combs and helmets among home-use LLLT options. 
Reviews of laser therapy for hair loss are mixed: a 2012 review found little evidence, 2014 reviews were mixed, and 2015 and 2017 reviews reported tentative benefit, with 10 of 11 trials in the 2017 review showing improvement.  Reviewers have called for larger, long-term, double-blind trials.

name: Hair fibres (Toppik)

angle.text: Users sprinkle Toppik-style fibres over thinning areas to make hair look denser within minutes. The fuller look is immediately visible and lasts until washed out; it disguises thinning rather than regrowing hair.

summary: Keratin-style cosmetic fibres that cling to existing hair to disguise thinning; a cover-up rather than a treatment, with a rare eye-injury case report.
note: A case report describes a fibre entering the eye and causing uveitis.
currentQuick:
Hair fibres such as Toppik are fine powders that bind to existing hair by static electricity to make thinning areas look fuller. They disguise hair loss rather than treating it.
Published research is limited to a 2017 microscopy analysis of five brands and a 2020 case report of eye injury.
How it works: Electrostatically charged fibres adhere to the hair shaft, thickening its appearance and reducing visible scalp. Effects last until washed out.
Risks and caveats: A 2020 case report described anterior uveitis after a fibre from a hair-building product entered the eye of a 73-year-old man.
deepLead:
Hair fibres, sold under brands such as Toppik, are cosmetic products made of fine fibres that adhere to the hair shaft by electrostatic attraction to disguise hair loss in men and women. 
A 2017 study used scanning electron microscopy and X-ray microanalysis to compare five brands of organic hair fibres.  No efficacy trials were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Anthralin (dithranol)

angle.text: Anthralin is a psoriasis ointment that is also discussed off-label for patchy alopecia areata, where users apply it to bald spots hoping for regrowth. Evidence for hair regrowth is tentative, and it is not a pattern-baldness treatment.

summary: A skin-irritant ointment from psoriasis care that is sometimes discussed for patchy alopecia areata; evidence for hair regrowth is tentative.
note: Stains skin and fabrics and can burn; used under clinician direction.
currentQuick:
Anthralin (dithranol) is a topical medication mainly used for psoriasis. In hair contexts it is discussed as an irritant treatment for alopecia areata.
Wikipedia reports only tentative evidence of benefit for alopecia areata, based on a 2013 review.
How it works: It is reported to accumulate in mitochondria and generate free radicals, slowing cell division; exact action is not fully understood.
Risks and caveats: Burning, irritation, temporary skin staining and permanent staining of clothes and fixtures are reported. In the UK it is a Pharmacy medicine.
deepLead:
Anthralin, also called dithranol, is a synthetic topical compound from the hydroxyanthrone and anthracene family, supplied as creams, ointments or pastes in strengths from roughly 0.1% to 2%. Its main established medical use is plaque psoriasis . In hair-related contexts it is discussed as a topical irritant treatment for alopecia areata, an autoimmune patchy hair-loss condition.
The English Wikipedia article notes only tentative evidence that it may help alopecia areata, citing a 2013 review . Documented effects include burning, irritation and temporary brown-to-purple staining of skin, and permanent staining of fabrics and bathroom fixtures .

name: Coppertone sunscreen

angle.text: Coppertone is a classic U.S. sunscreen and suntan-lotion brand used to tan with less burning and to limit sun-driven skin aging. UV filters as a class are well studied for photoprotection; brand-specific studies are essentially absent.

summary: Classic U.S. sunscreen and suntan-lotion brand famous for its pigtailed-girl ad; brand-specific clinical evidence is essentially absent.
note: Evidence concerns sunscreens generally, not this brand.
currentQuick:
Coppertone is a U.S. sun care brand that began as a 1944 suntan lotion and became known for its girl-and-puppy advertising.
It is now mostly a sunscreen line, owned by Beiersdorf after a 2019 announced acquisition from Bayer.
How it works: As a sunscreen brand it relies on UV filters; the sources reviewed do not list the filters used by specific products.
Risks and caveats: No brand-specific clinical safety studies were found. Early marketing emphasised tanning, and its history reflects changing sun-care norms.
deepLead:
Coppertone is a U.S. sun care brand. According to Wikipedia, it traces to a suntan lotion developed by pharmacist Benjamin Green in 1944, and it is described as the leading U.S. sun care brand . Its early marketing centred on tanning (slogan 'Tan, don't burn') rather than sunscreen as such .
Its best-known imagery is the 'Little Miss Coppertone' ad: a girl whose swimsuit is tugged by a puppy, exposing a tan line . Few clinical studies concern the brand specifically.

name: Piz Buin

angle.text: Piz Buin is a European sun care brand, descended from a 1946 glacier cream, used for holiday and outdoor sun protection and a steadier tan. Sunscreen filters as a class are well studied; for the brand itself only old mouse studies exist.

summary: Alpine-named European sun care brand dating to a 1946 glacier cream; only old mouse studies exist.
note: Evidence is for sunscreens generally, not this brand.
currentQuick:
Piz Buin is a European sun care brand tracing to Franz Greiter's 1946 Gletscher Crème.
It is named after an Alpine mountain.
How it works: It is a sunscreen brand; the sources reviewed do not detail its filters.
Risks and caveats: No human studies of the brand were found; only 1980s mouse experiments used it.
deepLead:
Piz Buin is a European sun care brand. According to Wikipedia, Austrian chemist Franz Greiter introduced a product called Gletscher Crème in 1946 that became the basis for Piz Buin, named after the mountain where Greiter reportedly got sunburned .
Published scientific use of the brand is limited to old animal experiments in which it served as a test sunscreen.

name: Bain de Soleil

angle.text: Bain de Soleil was a tanning gel brand, known for an orange gel and low-SPF products, used to build a deeper tan. It was discontinued in 2019 and is now mostly discussed as nostalgia, with no clinical studies on the brand.

summary: Discontinued 1925-born French-American tanning gel brand known for low SPF and nostalgia; no clinical evidence behind it.
note: Low-SPF tanning products offer limited sunburn protection by design.
currentQuick:
Bain de Soleil was a tanning-oriented sun care brand, famous for an orange gel launched in Paris in 1925.
Bayer discontinued it in December 2019.
How it works: It was positioned as a tanning aid with low SPF rather than a high-protection sunscreen.
Risks and caveats: No brand-specific studies were found. Low-SPF products give correspondingly lower sunburn protection.
deepLead:
Bain de Soleil ('sun bath' in French) was a tanning and sun care brand best known for an orange gel and low-SPF products. Wikipedia dates its origin to 1925, when Paris hairdresser Monsieur Antoine developed an orange gel tanning formula; Lanvin later introduced it in the U.S. . Bayer discontinued the brand in December 2019 .
A reference text from the AI-generated Grokipedia, which may contain errors, adds that a 2024 deal was announced for a relaunch; this is unverified here . No clinical studies of the brand are known.

name: Boots Soltan / star rating

angle.text: Users in the UK and Ireland read the Boots star rating to pick sunscreens with higher UVA protection relative to UVB, since UVA is tied to skin aging and pigmentation. It is a labelling method rather than a product, and the Soltan range itself is not described in the sources reviewed.

summary: UK/Ireland star label showing a sunscreen's UVA-to-UVB protection ratio, from Boots.
note: Stars describe UVA ratio, not total protection; read SPF as well.
currentQuick:
The Boots star rating is a UK and Ireland label for the ratio of UVA to UVB protection in a sunscreen.
It runs up to five stars and was developed with Brian Diffey's work.
How it works: An in vitro test compares UVA to UVB protection, with pre-irradiation in the revised method.
Risks and caveats: Studies note labelling differences between regions and products with identical SPF.
deepLead:
The Boots star rating is a UK and Ireland labelling system for the UVA protection of sunscreens, expressed relative to UVB protection. Wikipedia describes it as a proprietary in vitro method in which five stars is the highest UVA ratio and one star the lowest . Soltan is a sunscreen range from Boots; the sources reviewed do not describe it.
Brian Diffey at Newcastle University did the original work, and Boots in Nottingham developed the method, which many UK manufacturers adopted .

name: Tinosorb S (bemotrizinol)

angle.text: Skincare fans seek out Tinosorb S for its broad-spectrum, photostable UV protection in sunscreens and daily creams, mainly from EU and Asian products. It is well characterised as a UV filter, with US availability still pending in the sources reviewed.

summary: A photostable broad-spectrum UV filter common in EU and Asian sunscreens, with US availability still pending in the sources reviewed.
note: Not in the US OTC monograph per the cited sources; status may have changed.
currentQuick:
Tinosorb S is a chemical UV filter that absorbs both UVB and UVA light. It is common in European, Australian and Asian sunscreens and is often discussed in skincare communities as a reason to seek out non-US products.
Research mostly covers formulation behaviour: a 2001 study reported it helped stabilise avobenzone and another filter under light. Trials of the filter alone on appearance outcomes were not found.
How it works: It absorbs ultraviolet photons and releases the energy as heat, and is described as highly photostable.
Risks and caveats: Photoallergy to sunscreen filters is described as rare in a 2010 study. A 2023 study measured how much is absorbed, as part of work toward possible US OTC inclusion. Environmental monitoring has detected UV filters in coastal waters.
deepLead:
Bemotrizinol, sold by BASF as Tinosorb S and known by the INCI name bis-ethylhexyloxyphenol methoxyphenyl triazine, is an oil-soluble organic ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens and daily skincare. It absorbs across the UVB and UVA ranges, with absorption peaks reported near 310 nm and 340-345 nm.
It is used widely in European, Australian and Asian sunscreens, and is often described as photostable. Laboratory work from 2001 reported that adding it to formulations helped stabilise the filters avobenzone and ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate under irradiation. In the United States it has not been part of the over-the-counter sunscreen monograph; a 2023 pharmacokinetic study was published as part of work toward its possible inclusion.
Evidence on the ingredient consists mainly of formulation, photostability and absorption studies rather than trials measuring sunburn or skin-cancer outcomes for the filter alone.

name: Tinosorb M (bisoctrizole)

angle.text: Tinosorb M is a hybrid organic and particulate UV filter used in European and Asian sunscreens for broad UVA and UVB coverage, which users value for long-term skin protection. Published work focuses on formulation and contact allergy rather than appearance outcomes.

summary: A hybrid organic/particulate UV filter in European and Asian sunscreens; reported contact allergies have been traced to a surfactant in its dispersion.
note: Not in the US OTC monograph per the cited source.
currentQuick:
Tinosorb M is a broad-spectrum UV filter supplied as fine particles. It is described as working through both absorption and scattering, and it appears in sunscreens sold in the EU and other regions.
The published literature is mostly allergy reports and lab or ex vivo work. No trials were found testing it alone on appearance outcomes.
How it works: Its benzotriazole structure absorbs UV and dissipates the energy as heat; particles are also said to scatter some light.
Risks and caveats: Dermatology reports describe allergic contact dermatitis, attributed in several cases to decyl glucoside in the dispersion. A 2010 study found true photoallergy to sunscreens to be rare.
deepLead:
Bisoctrizole, marketed by BASF as Tinosorb M (INCI name methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol), is an ultraviolet filter described as a hybrid: it is a benzotriazole organic molecule supplied as microfine particles in water-based dispersions, so it is said to act both by absorbing and by scattering UV light. It is used in sunscreens for broad UVA and UVB coverage.
Published research on the ingredient includes contact-allergy case reports and series, photopatch-testing recommendations, ex vivo skin studies of an organo-mineral sunblock, and environmental monitoring. Several dermatology reports attribute allergic reactions to Tinosorb M to decyl glucoside, a surfactant in the commercial dispersion, rather than the filter itself.

name: Uvinul A Plus

angle.text: Uvinul A Plus is a photostable UVA filter found in EU sunscreens, sought by users who want strong UVA protection against skin aging and pigmentation. Published material covers mainly chemistry and metabolism rather than appearance outcomes.

summary: A photostable organic UVA filter used in EU sunscreens, with little published beyond chemistry and metabolism.
note: Not a US sunscreen active per Wikipedia.
currentQuick:
Uvinul A Plus is a UVA filter found in some sunscreens, particularly in Europe. It is described as photostable.
Sources are thin: chemistry papers and a 2020 human metabolism study, with no appearance trials.
How it works: It absorbs UVA light, peaking near 354 nm, and dissipates the energy.
Risks and caveats: The EU safety committee flagged a manufacturing impurity (di-n-hexyl phthalate) and recommended limits. Human metabolism was studied after oral and dermal doses in 2020.
deepLead:
Uvinul A Plus is BASF's trade name for diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB, also sold as Parsol DHHB), an organic UVA-absorbing sunscreen filter. It is described as photostable and is used in sunscreens and other cosmetics in the European Union at up to 10 percent.
Available research is chemical and toxicokinetic: a 2017 photophysics study and a 2020 human metabolism study. No trials of appearance outcomes were found.

name: Uvinul T 150 (ethylhexyl triazone)

angle.text: Ethylhexyl triazone is a UVB filter used in EU sunscreens to raise SPF, so users look for it in products aimed at preventing burns and sun damage. Published work is mostly on formulation and environmental behaviour, not appearance.

summary: A UVB sunscreen filter used to boost SPF in EU products, with little published beyond formulation and environmental studies.
note: Not a US sunscreen active per the cited source.
currentQuick:
Uvinul T 150 is a UVB filter used in some sunscreens, mainly outside the US, where it helps reach higher SPF values.
Published work is mostly formulation tests and environmental monitoring; no clinical studies were found.
How it works: It absorbs UVB light (peak near 314 nm) and is described as photostable.
Risks and caveats: No human clinical safety trials were found in the sources reviewed. Environmental studies have detected triazine filters in sediment, dust and tested aquatic organisms.
deepLead:
Ethylhexyl triazone, marketed by BASF as Uvinul T 150, is an oil-soluble organic UVB filter used in sunscreens, typically to raise SPF. A Grokipedia summary reports an absorption peak near 314 nm, a permitted EU level of up to 5 percent, and no approval as a US sunscreen active.
Published work involving the ingredient is mainly product-testing and environmental. A 2011 study compared fifteen European sunscreens of identical label SPF under natural sunlight, and environmental studies have measured triazine UV filters in sediments, indoor dust and marine organisms.

name: Mexoryl SX (ecamsule)

angle.text: Mexoryl SX is L'Oreal's UVA filter, used in sunscreens and daily moisturisers by people aiming to limit sun-driven skin aging. It is among the more studied filters, with human photoprotection and absorption data.

summary: L'Oreal's long-studied UVA filter, with human photoprotection and absorption data.
note: A 2019 JAMA trial found measurable blood levels after maximal use.
currentQuick:
Mexoryl SX is a UVA filter developed by L'Oreal and used in products such as Anthelios and La Roche-Posay sunscreens. It is one of the few newer UVA filters available in the US.
It has more human data than most newer filters, including studies on UVA-induced skin changes, pigmentation and photoaging markers.
How it works: It absorbs UVA (peak near 345 nm) and is described as photostable; it dissolves in the water phase of formulations.
Risks and caveats: A 2019 JAMA trial found it was detectable in blood after maximal-use application, above the FDA threshold for further testing; the paper does not conclude this indicates harm. Photoallergy to sunscreens is described as rare.
deepLead:
Ecamsule, known commercially as Mexoryl SX (INCI name terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid), is a water-soluble UVA filter developed by L'Oreal. Grokipedia states it absorbs with a peak near 345 nm and was developed and patented in 1982.
It has been studied more extensively than many newer filters. A 1998 study reported protection of human skin against repeated sub-erythemal UVA doses, a 2008 review summarised clinical results of Mexoryl SX sunscreens, and a 2019 JAMA trial found that ecamsule and three other sunscreen ingredients reached plasma concentrations above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold under maximal-use conditions.

name: Mexoryl XL (drometrizole trisiloxane)

angle.text: Mexoryl XL is L'Oreal's broad-spectrum filter, usually paired with Mexoryl SX in sunscreens sold outside the US, and is sought for long-term UV protection of facial skin. Standalone research is limited.

summary: L'Oreal's broad UVA/UVB filter, usually paired with Mexoryl SX; sold outside the US with little standalone research.
note: Not approved in the US per Wikipedia.
currentQuick:
Mexoryl XL is a UV filter from L'Oreal that covers both UVB and UVA. It is usually combined with Mexoryl SX in European and Asian sunscreens.
Sources are thin: studies tested finished sunscreens, not the filter alone.
How it works: It absorbs UV with peaks near 303 and 344 nm.
Risks and caveats: Sources reviewed contain no specific safety findings for this filter. It is not approved in the US.
deepLead:
Drometrizole trisiloxane, sold by L'Oreal as Mexoryl XL, is a lipophilic benzotriazole-derived UV filter that absorbs in both UVB and UVA, with peaks reported at 303 nm and 344 nm. It is often combined with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX).
Wikipedia reports it is approved in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan but not in the United States. Dedicated literature is sparse; most studies cited here tested L'Oreal sunscreens containing it alongside other filters.

name: Iscotrizinol (Uvasorb HEB)

angle.text: Iscotrizinol is a very photostable UVB filter common in East Asian sunscreens, where users favour it for daily facial protection. Human clinical research under its own name is limited.

summary: A very photostable triazine UVB filter common in East Asian sunscreens, with little human clinical research under its own name.
note: Approval status varies by country; no clinical trials of the filter alone found.
currentQuick:
Iscotrizinol is an organic sunscreen filter sold as Uvasorb HEB. It absorbs UVB and some UVA light and is described as very photostable.
It appears in some Asian-market sunscreens. Whether it can be sold depends on the country, and a US application was reported as pending.
How it works: It absorbs ultraviolet light, peaking near 310 nm, and the absorbed energy is released within the film on the skin.
Risks and caveats: No clinical safety trials specific to iscotrizinol were found. Environmental studies of UV filters in general are ongoing. Regulatory approval varies by country.
deepLead:
Iscotrizinol, listed in ingredient labels as diethylhexyl butamido triazone and sold under the trade name Uvasorb HEB, is an organic (chemical) ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens. It belongs to the triazine family, absorbs mainly UVB and some short-wave UVA light, and has its peak absorption near 310 nm.
Encyclopedic sources describe it as an unusually photostable filter, meaning it loses little of its protective ability under prolonged light exposure. Its approval status differs between countries; one encyclopedia entry notes that a US application was still pending.
No published human clinical trial in the sources reviewed here tests iscotrizinol on its own as a sunscreen ingredient. Published research that mentions it is mostly analytical or environmental, for example studies measuring UV filters in cosmetics or in the water-flea Daphnia magna.

name: Parsol 1789 (avobenzone)

angle.text: Avobenzone is the standard UVA filter in most chemical sunscreens, used to reduce sun-driven skin aging and pigmentation. It needs stabilisers because it degrades in sunlight, and its UVA absorption is well characterised.

summary: The standard UVA filter in most chemical sunscreens, effective but needing stabilizers because it degrades in sunlight.
note: Absorbed into the bloodstream in FDA-sponsored trials; FDA has not classed it as GRASE.
currentQuick:
Avobenzone, often labelled Parsol 1789, is the main UVA-absorbing filter in chemical sunscreens. It is used at up to 3 percent in the US and 5 percent in the EU.
It breaks down in sunlight unless stabilized, so formulators pair it with other filters such as octocrylene.
How it works: It absorbs UVA light around 357-360 nm and dissipates the energy, mostly as heat.
Risks and caveats: Clinical trials found it enters the bloodstream after application, with unknown clinical significance. The FDA has said more safety data are needed for GRASE status. Palau has banned it over reef concerns.
deepLead:
Avobenzone, sold under trade names including Parsol 1789, Eusolex 9020 and Escalol 517, is an oil-soluble organic filter used in sunscreens to absorb ultraviolet A (UVA) light, with peak absorption near 357 to 360 nm. It is a dibenzoylmethane derivative with the formula C20H22O3.
It is among the most widely used UVA filters. In the United States it is permitted at up to 3 percent in over-the-counter sunscreens, and in the EU at up to 5 percent. A known property is its photoinstability: it can lose absorbance under sunlight, so formulators pair it with stabilizers such as octocrylene.
Two randomized clinical trials published in JAMA found that avobenzone and other tested active ingredients entered the bloodstream after sunscreen application; the studies did not assess whether this causes harm.

name: Octocrylene

angle.text: Octocrylene is a UVB filter used mainly to keep avobenzone from breaking down, so it appears in many sunscreens used for daily skin protection. Its absorption, benzophenone formation and reef effects are still being studied.

summary: A photostable UVB filter used mainly to keep avobenzone from breaking down, with open questions over absorption, benzophenone formation and reef effects.
note: Systemically absorbed in trials; can degrade into benzophenone; restricted in Palau and the US Virgin Islands.
currentQuick:
Octocrylene is a UVB-absorbing sunscreen ingredient that also stabilizes avobenzone. It is common in chemical sunscreens and in cosmetics with SPF.
It has drawn attention for being absorbed into the body, for slowly forming benzophenone in products, and for environmental concerns.
How it works: It absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA light and is itself largely photostable, so it helps keep other filters from degrading.
Risks and caveats: Clinical trials detected it in plasma above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold, with unknown clinical significance. Some places restrict it for reef-protection reasons.
deepLead:
Octocrylene is an organic ultraviolet filter and photostabilizer used in sunscreens and other cosmetics. It is an ester (C24H27NO2) that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA light, and it is commonly added to stabilize avobenzone.
It has been the subject of scrutiny on three fronts: systemic absorption seen in US clinical trials, slow degradation into benzophenone in stored products, and environmental effects reported in laboratory studies of corals and other marine organisms.
Several jurisdictions that restrict reef-toxic sunscreen ingredients, such as Palau and the US Virgin Islands, have included it in their restrictions.

name: Zinc oxide mineral sunscreen

chain: Mineral filter blocks UVA and UVB
angle.text: Zinc oxide sunscreens are used by people who want broad-spectrum, photostable protection, often for sensitive or acne-prone skin and daily facial use. It is a well-studied filter, and the visible white cast and nanoparticle debate are its main discussion points.

summary: A photostable broad-spectrum mineral sunscreen filter, FDA-GRASE, whose main trade-off is white cast and nanoparticle debate.
note: Nanoparticle penetration studies found minimal skin penetration; white cast is the usual complaint.
currentQuick:
Zinc oxide is a mineral sunscreen filter that covers UVA and UVB. It is one of two filters the FDA considers generally recognized as safe and effective.
Its appearance on the skin is the usual complaint, which is why nanoscale versions exist.
How it works: Particles on the skin absorb UV light and also reflect and scatter some of it.
Risks and caveats: Studies of nanoparticle zinc oxide on human skin found very low penetration. Laboratory work has examined zinc release under UV and combinations with organic filters.
deepLead:
Zinc oxide mineral sunscreen uses zinc oxide, an inorganic (mineral) compound, as its active ultraviolet filter. Zinc oxide protects against both UVA and UVB light and, with titanium dioxide, is one of the two mineral filters used in sunscreens.
Wikipedia describes it as the broadest-spectrum UVA and UVB absorber approved by the US FDA for sunscreen and as photostable. As of 2021 zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were the only sunscreen filters the FDA categorized as generally recognized as safe and effective (GRASE).
Much published research concerns nanoparticulate zinc oxide, which is used to avoid the white appearance of conventional mineral products. Studies using skin-penetration assays and in vivo microscopy have examined whether the particles pass through human skin.

name: Titanium dioxide sunscreen

angle.text: Titanium dioxide sunscreens are used for mineral-based protection, strongest against UVB and partly UVA, and are often paired with zinc oxide for fuller coverage. It is one of two filters the FDA classed as generally recognised as safe and effective as of 2021.

summary: A mineral UV filter, FDA-GRASE, strong on UVB and partly UVA, usually paired with zinc oxide.
note: Inhaled TiO2 dust is IARC Group 2B; IARC advises against sprayable sunscreens.
currentQuick:
Titanium dioxide is a mineral sunscreen filter used mainly for UVB and part of UVA protection. It is usually paired with zinc oxide.
It is one of two filters the FDA treats as generally recognized as safe and effective.
How it works: Fine particles on the skin absorb UV light and scatter some of it.
Risks and caveats: A pilot study looked at skin absorption. Inhaled TiO2 dust is classified Group 2B by IARC, which is why sprays draw caution. White cast is a common cosmetic complaint.
deepLead:
Titanium dioxide sunscreen uses titanium dioxide (TiO2), an inorganic mineral, as an ultraviolet filter. With zinc oxide it is one of the two mineral filters in sunscreens, and the two were the only filters the US FDA classed as generally recognized as safe and effective as of 2021.
Wikipedia says titanium dioxide offers good protection but does not fully cover the UVA range. Sunscreens use ultrafine (nanoscale) forms, often combined with ultrafine zinc oxide, and some add iron oxide to block visible light.
Published work on the ingredient includes a 1990s pilot study of absorption through human skin, a yeast-based photosafety model, and patents on mineral powder blends.

name: Oxybenzone-free sunscreen

chain: Still filters UV with other agents
angle.text: Shoppers pick oxybenzone-free sunscreens to keep daily UV protection while avoiding an ingredient tied to allergy, hormone and reef concerns, which are debated. It is a label category rather than one ingredient, and protection depends on the filters used instead.

summary: A label category for sunscreens without benzophenone-3, driven by allergy, hormone and reef concerns that are debated.
note: Evidence on benefits of avoiding oxybenzone is limited; restrictions exist in Hawaii and Palau.
currentQuick:
Oxybenzone-free sunscreens leave out benzophenone-3, a UV filter linked to allergic reactions, hormone-related concerns and coral studies.
The label is a consumer category, and regulators in places such as Hawaii and Palau restrict oxybenzone products.
How it works: Instead of oxybenzone they use other filters, often zinc oxide, titanium dioxide or other organic filters.
Risks and caveats: A 2022 study found multiple benzophenone filters in US sunscreens, which tested for several benzophenones besides oxybenzone. Public health bodies say sun-exposure cancer risk outweighs unproven filter toxicity concerns.
deepLead:
Oxybenzone-free sunscreen refers to sunscreens formulated without oxybenzone (benzophenone-3, BP-3), an organic UV filter that has been the subject of safety and environmental debate. The term is a marketing and consumer category rather than a single ingredient.
Oxybenzone covers UVB and short-wave UVA. Wikipedia reports it is a known sensitizer that can cause allergic contact dermatitis, that it is absorbed through skin, and that the European Chemicals Agency identified it as an endocrine disruptor in September 2025; it also notes that studies have linked it to coral harm, while critics say many of those studies lacked controls or realistic conditions.
In the US the FDA lists oxybenzone as Category III, meaning insufficient data to class it as generally recognized as safe and effective, though it remains legal. Hawaii, Palau and other places have restricted sales of oxybenzone products.
